tip: On hindsight: στερνή μου γνώση να σ' είχα πρώτα (sterni mu gnosi na s' ikha prota) = my late-coming wisdom, if only I'd had you first – addressed to hindsight itself.
Healthy skepticism: όπου ακούς πολλά κεράσια, κράτα και μικρό καλάθι (opu akus polla kerasia, krata ke mikro kalathi) = where you hear of many cherries, carry a small basket too.
Two of a kind: βρήκε ο τέντζερης το καπάκι (vrike o tendzeris to kapaki = the pot found its lid).
Losing it: βγαίνω από τα ρούχα μου (vyeno apo ta rukha mu = I come out of my clothes) = to lose your temper.
Cutting ties: ρίχνω μαύρη πέτρα πίσω μου (rikhno mavri petra piso mu = I throw a black stone behind me) = break with a place for good.
Exhausting effort: μου έβγαλε το λάδι (mu evghale to ladhi = it drew out my oil) = it wore me out.
Total confusion: χάνω τα αυγά και τα καλάθια (khano ta avgha ke ta kalathia = I lose eggs and baskets) = lose all track.
On forgetting: όποιος δεν έχει μυαλό, έχει ποδάρια (opios dhen ekhi mialo, ekhi podharia) = whoever has no brains has legs – your feet pay for what your head forgot.
The ending -ώντας means 'while doing': περπατώντας (perpatondas = walking) adds an action running alongside the main verb.
Το γεγονός ότι (to yeghonos oti = the fact that) turns a whole clause into a noun, here the subject of the sentence.
Αυτό που (afto pu = the thing that) opens the sentence with the topic, putting the emphasis up front.
Το να + verb turns an action into a subject: το να παραδεχτείς (to na paradhekhtis = admitting) works like English '-ing', as in 'admitting takes courage'.
Two -οντας verbs can stack for things happening at once: δουλεύοντας (dhulevondas = working) runs alongside the main verb.
To contrast explanations Greek uses δεν είναι ότι... είναι ότι... (dhen ine oti... ine oti...) = it's not that... it's that... – the frame sets up the correction before it lands.
Έχοντας plus a past form = 'having done': έχοντας χάσει (ekhondas khasi = having lost) puts the finished action first.
Endings in -μένος/-μένο mark a lasting state: χτισμένο (khtismeno = built) is the result of building, not the act.
Δεν ήταν η αποτυχία... αλλά (dhen itan i apotikhia... alla = it wasn't the failure... but) names the wrong candidate first – Greek's way of spotlighting what really mattered.
A -οντας verb up front gives the background: διαβάζοντας (dhiavazondas = reading) sets the scene before the result.
Το να + verb makes an action something you can fear or want: το να αποτύχω (to na apotikho = failing) is the thing feared here.
Endings in -μένος/-μένη describe a state: καθισμένη (kathismeni = seated) takes the -η form to match a woman.
Στο να... και στο να... lines up two actions for comparison: στο να είσαι (sto na ise = to being) is the first of the pair.
Putting a -μένο word first adds weight: γραμμένο (grammeno = written) opens with the note's state before we hear what it is.
Προσποιούμενος (prospiumenos = pretending) has the passive -ούμενος (-umenos) ending but an active meaning – some Greek verbs only come in the passive shape.
Έχοντας plus a past form = experience already behind you: έχοντας ζήσει (ekhondas zisi = having lived).
Το να + verb turns an action into the subject: το να αλλάξεις (to na allaxis = to change your mind) heads the sentence.
The -μένος ending can describe a feeling too: πληγωμένος (plighomenos = wounded) sets his condition up front.
A -μένα word up front describes the noun coming next: σκαλισμένα (skalismena = carved) tells you about τα σκαλοπάτια (ta skalopatia = the steps).
Το να ζητάς (to na zitas = asking) works as the subject of the sentence, the way English uses '-ing'.
Έχοντας δει (ekhondas dhi = having seen) sums up past experience that explains the habit he learned.
An -οντας verb sets the scene for the main clause: διασχίζοντας τα σύνορα (dhiaskhizondas ta sinora = crossing the border), I felt... – Greek's 'while doing X' opener.
